items.title: 52115_Danny Barker oral history interview
items.q: Picou, Tio, all them people down there could talk a little French.

ctx.x: Big-Eye Louis [Nelson] was a great clarinet player, who was somewhat of a rival of Tio. Big-Eye Louis and Picou, they were masters of that style of playing, that improvisation...
Was Jay-Joe(?) from here? A clarinet player named Jay-Joe(?).

items.title: Danny Barker — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

ctx.x: Kid Rena. Buddy Petit. Chris Kelly. Every element of Chicago had its halls. Every element of Chicago had its musicians who played for them halls. You wouldn’t expect Chris Kelly to play them funky lowdown blues where Piron played, and Piron wouldn’t play the joints where Chris Kelly played, or Kid Rena or Buddy. You

understand? Each level of society had their music. It was a well calculated thing. It was well practiced. Certain musicians played for certain people. That changed the whole saxophone scene. It was David Jones. That’s what Lee Collins tells me, and I could see it. I could see it, how he mastered that tenor saxophone. When I get to New York, I really see what . . . He had started playing here. But New Orleans is never famous for famous tenor players, because this was the clarinet town. Had clarinets after…

items.title: Danny Barker Interview, 1959-06-30
items.q: He was real great in the style, and I was Piku, was great.

ctx.x: Willie Humphrey, the one that's working with Paul now. Earl Humphrey's brother. He impressed me, but he lived uptown and never had a chance much to him. And he's the one that impressed me, I thought he was a master. There were others, like Big Al Lloyd, who was always in the same track in the summer of retirement. He played if he got a chance. I worked with him, I know him at Twy, and Walter DeCoult, four of us at the Bungalow. Out on the Shellback Road, I worked a couple of months out there with them. He was…
